o: Intercostal collateral branches have no cutaneous branch
They supply muscle, parietal pleura and periosteum. (Last's p. 244)
The first intercostal nerve has a lateral cutaneous branch
It supplies no skin at all. (Last's p. 245)
At the front of the space the intercostal nerve crosses in front of the internal thoracic artery
At the back it crosses behind the posterior intercostal artery. (Last's p. 245)
In thoracotomy the periosteum is stripped from the lower half of the rib
From the upper half, away from the bundle. (Last's p. 244)
There are no anterior intercostal arteries in the last two spaces
(Last's p. 246)
The anterior intercostal arteries are larger than the posterior
The posterior are larger. (Last's p. 246)
The left superior intercostal vein runs superficial to the vagus and deep to the phrenic
Over the aortic arch. (Last's p. 246)
The first intercostal space drains into the superior intercostal vein
It drains via the supreme intercostal vein to vertebral or brachiocephalic. (Last's p. 246)
The suprapleural membrane is not attached to the neck of the first rib
T1 crosses there. (Last's p. 246)
The suprapleural membrane projects high into the root of the neck
It is flat in the plane of the inlet. (Last's p. 246)
The supreme intercostal vein lies between the superior intercostal artery and the sympathetic trunk
On the neck of the first rib. (Last's p. 245-6)
The superior intercostal artery supplies the upper three spaces
It supplies the upper two. (Last's p. 245)
The right crus attaches to L1–3 and the left to L1–2
(Last's p. 247)
Muscle fibres arise from the median arcuate ligament
They arise from the medial and lateral but not the median arcuate. (Last's p. 247)
The longest diaphragmatic fibres arise from the ninth costal cartilage
The shortest from the xiphisternum. (Last's p. 247)
The aortic opening lies within the diaphragm
It lies behind it, behind the median arcuate ligament. (Last's p. 248)
The oesophageal opening lies behind the seventh left costal cartilage
At T10. (Last's p. 248)
The left phrenic nerve passes through the caval foramen
The right does; the left pierces the muscle of the left dome. (Last's p. 248)
The part of the right crus left of the oesophagus is supplied by the left phrenic
(Last's p. 248)
The lower intercostal nerves give motor fibres to the peripheral diaphragm
Only proprioceptive fibres; motor is solely phrenic. (Last's p. 248)
About 55% of diaphragm fibres are slow twitch
65% of intercostal fibres. (Last's p. 248)
Deep inspiration can depress the central tendon from T8 to T11
Only to T9. (Last's p. 248)
Bochdalek hernia is commoner on the left
Liver pressure may close the right earlier. (Last's p. 249)
The diaphragm is active in forced expiration
It is wholly passive in expiration. (Last's p. 249)

questions.s: Concerning the phrenic and vagus in the thorax (Last's):
o: About two-thirds of phrenic fibres are motor
(Last's p. 259)
The phrenic nerve supplies the visceral pericardium
It supplies fibrous and parietal serous pericardium, not viscera. (Last's p. 259)
The right phrenic nerve is in contact with venous structures throughout
(Last's p. 259)
The left vagus crosses the aortic arch superficial to the left superior intercostal vein
It crosses deep to it. (Last's p. 259)
Last's says intercostals matter more for thoracic twisting than respiration
(Last's p. 249)
In quiet respiration expiration is mainly by the internal intercostals
Expiration is largely passive. (Last's p. 249)
During coughing the trachea narrows 10% at the instant the cords open
After a 30% widening. (Last's p. 259)
The tracheal bifurcation rises during swallowing
It does not move; the trachea stretches. (Last's p. 259)
The thoracic duct has no valves at its termination
Blood may enter the terminal inch or two. (Last's p. 277)
The thoracic duct begins at T10
At T12, between aorta and azygos. (Last's p. 277)
The thoracic duct crosses behind the oesophagus to its left side
Reaching the left side in the superior mediastinum. (Last's p. 277)
Mediastinal lymph trunks usually join the thoracic duct
They usually open directly into the brachiocephalic veins. (Last's p. 277)
The azygos arches over the right bronchus at T4
(Last's p. 278)
The hemiazygos veins join the azygos at T6 and T7
At T8 and T9. (Last's p. 278)
The accessory hemiazygos receives the left bronchial veins
(Last's p. 278)
The azygos begins as a functional channel from the IVC
That part is usually a fibrous cord; it functionally begins at the ascending lumbar–subcostal union. (Last's p. 277)
The greater splanchnic nerve arises from ganglia 5 to 9
Lesser 10–11, least 12. (Last's p. 278)
The grey ramus usually lies lateral to the white ramus
It usually lies medial. (Last's p. 278)
The oesophageal plexuses are vagal
Not sympathetic. (Last's p. 278)
The stellate ganglion lies posterolateral to the vertebral artery
The inferior cervical ganglion lies posteromedial to it. (Last's p. 278)
The visceral pleura has only an autonomic supply
It is insensitive to ordinary stimuli. (Last's p. 279)
The pulmonary ligament supports the lung
It is neither related to the lung nor a ligament; it is dead space for the inferior pulmonary vein. (Last's p. 279)
The pleura crosses the twelfth rib at the lateral border of erector spinae
Leaving a triangle behind the kidney's upper pole. (Last's p. 279)
The pleura crosses the midaxillary line at the eighth rib
At the tenth; the midclavicular line at the eighth. (Last's p. 279)
The innermost intercostal fibres cross only one intercostal space
They cross more than one. (Last's p. 244)
The posterior intercostal membrane extends from the sternum to the costal angle
It extends from the angle to the superior costotransverse ligament. (Last's p. 244)
Transversus thoracis digitations reach costal cartilages 1 to 7
Cartilages 2 to 6. (Last's p. 244)
Between subcostals and innermost intercostals the intercostal nerves and vessels touch the pleura
(Last's p. 244)
The oesophageal opening may lie in the midline, its developmental position
It is usually an inch left of it. (Last's p. 248)
The superior epigastric vessels pass between the xiphisternal and costal fibres
(Last's p. 248)
Connective tissue around the caval opening comes from the oesophageal mesentery
(Last's p. 249)
The hemiazygos vein passes through the left crus
(Last's p. 248)
The right vagus lies on the trachea deep to the arch of the azygos
(Last's p. 259)
The left phrenic nerve crosses the aortic arch behind the vagus
It crosses in front of the vagus. (Last's p. 259)
The thymus lies behind the pericardium
It lies in front of the pericardium and great vessels. (Last's p. 260)
The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply only the larynx
They also supply trachea and oesophagus. (Last's p. 259)
